lesson.title: hatte & war: The Fortress Pasts
lesson.subtitle: haben and sein keep their simple pasts: hatte ↔ had, war ↔ was — the -te is your -ed

hook.title: The Two Verbs That Never Surrendered
hook.content: Topic 18 handed you the Perfekt — ge- participles closing brackets everywhere. But two verbs refused the surrender. Storytelling reaches for the old simple pasts first: ich hatte, ich war. The Perfekt versions, 'ich habe gehabt' and 'ich bin gewesen', are heard in everyday speech too, but they are not the default for 'I had' and 'I was'. These are the fortress verbs — the last place the ancient past tense lives in daily German. And the ending on the fortress wall spells its own history: hatte ↔ had. That -te is the same dental suffix as your -ed (Old English hæfde — 'I had' — ends in -de). German never stopped conjugating with the ending English still wears.

footnotes.title: The Dental Suffix
footnotes.content: The weak-past ending -te (machte, sagte, hatte) and the English -ed are one and the same Proto-Germanic dental suffix *-dē. English wore it as -ed/-d, German as -te — machte ↔ made is not a coincidence but a shared inheritance doing paperwork.

pattern.title: The Fortress Wall, Person by Person
pattern.content: haben: ich hatte ↔ I had, du hattest ↔ thou hadst, er hatte ↔ he had, wir hatten ↔ we had. sein: ich war ↔ I was, du warst ↔ thou wast, er war ↔ he was, wir waren ↔ we were. The storytelling frames: Gestern hatte ich keine Zeit (yesterday I had no time). Das Haus war alt (the house was old). Wir waren in Berlin (we were in Berlin). One honest note: the Perfekt forms exist — gehabt, gewesen — and you will hear them in everyday speech too, but the simple pasts remain the default for telling a story.
pattern.linguist_note: war ↔ was is the *wes- root from the sein lesson's three-verb trench coat — and hattest ↔ hadst is the same -st you have drilled since the Shakespeare lesson, riding on the dental suffix. Two histories, one ending.

exercises.prompt: The fortress wall — match each English past with its German twin:
exercises.target_answer: ich hatte, ich war, du hattest, wir waren, ich war jung, wir waren gesund
exercises.meaning: I had, I was, thou hadst, we were, I was young, we were healthy
exercises.explanation: hatte ↔ had (one dental suffix, -te ↔ -ed) and war ↔ was — the fortress pasts of haben and sein, carrying the storyteller's adjectives: jung, gesund, stark, schwach.

exercises.prompt: Storytelling check: 'Gestern _____ ich keine Zeit.' (yesterday I HAD no time):
exercises.explanation: Speech keeps the simple past: hatte, never habe gehabt. The fortress verb does its own storytelling.

exercises.prompt: Say where you were yesterday: 'Du _____ gestern in Berlin.' (you were):
exercises.meaning: Du warst gestern in Berlin = you were in Berlin yesterday
exercises.explanation: du warst ↔ thou wast — the *wes- root with the -st ending, both words ancient in both languages. And the strong pasts pair with war in every story: fallen fiel, springen sprang, treten trat, schlagen schlug, stehlen stahl.

exercises.prompt: Which English word is the true twin of 'hatte'?
exercises.explanation: Old English hæfde — 'had' — wears the same dental past suffix as hatte. The fortress pasts are one fortress.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the storyteller's line: 'Yesterday I had no time'
exercises.meaning: Gestern hatte ich keine Zeit = yesterday I had no time

vocab_hints.note: haben's simple past — the fortress form
kein before a noun — the none-word

exercises.explanation: Gestern fronts the adverb, hatte holds position 2 — the fortress past running a verb-second main clause.

summary.outcome: Tell yesterday's story with hatte and war, and explain why habe gehabt never shows up in speech.

use_example.german: Gestern hatte ich keine Zeit, aber der Kaffee war gut.
use_example.english: Yesterday I had no time, but the coffee was good.

summary.takeaway: hatte ↔ had and war ↔ was: the -te/-ed dental suffix shared, the fortress pasts of haben und sein.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: konnte & musste — the frozen pasts of the modals, English's own could/should/would.

kind.context_translation: The child plays in the garden.
kind.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kindą, related to the root of English kin — 'of the family'. The t → z shift never fired here; the d hardened to t instead. [wiktionary]

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

jung.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *jungaz — the twin of English young (see der Junge). [wiktionary]

stark.etymology_derivation: From Old High German stark, Proto-West Germanic *stark; the everyday English word stark, as in stark naked, is the very same Germanic word. [wiktionary]

schwach.context_phrase: Nach der Krankheit war er schwach.
schwach.context_translation: After the illness he was weak.
schwach.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German swach, Proto-West Germanic *swak; the English cousins are the dialectal word swack, meaning nimble or lively, and Scots swack. [wiktionary]

gesund.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *sundaz — the same root as English sound, as in safe and sound. [wiktionary]

fallen.context_phrase: Das Glas ist vom Tisch gefallen.
fallen.context_translation: The glass fell off the table.
fallen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *fallaną; the page lists English fall among the akin forms — a class 7 strong verb on both sides: fell and fiel, fallen and gefallen. [wiktionary]

springen.context_phrase: Das Kind springt über den Bach.
springen.context_translation: The child jumps over the brook.
springen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *springaną (PIE *sprenǵʰ-) — English spring is the documented cognate; strong verb: sprang, gesprungen. [wiktionary]

treten.context_translation: Do not step in the puddle.
treten.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *trudaną — English tread is the documented cognate; the same class 5 ablaut: tritt, trat ↔ tread, trod. [wiktionary]

schlagen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *slahaną — English slay (Old English slēan) and slog are documented cognates; strong verb: schlug, geschlagen. [wiktionary]

stehlen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *stelana, the same root as English steal; both keep the class-4 ablaut — steal, stole, stolen mirrors stehlen, stahl, gestohlen. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
